relationship: Moses called the man of God in a prayer and a blessing
rationale: The psalm heading calls Moses the man of God. Deuteronomy uses the same title to introduce his blessing of Israel before his death. The connection concerns the two texts' Mosaic framing; it does not date the psalm to that final blessing.

relationship: The Creator endures beyond the created world
rationale: Psalm 89 places God's existence before mountains and the formed world. Psalm 101 contrasts the founded earth and heavens, which will perish, with the Lord who remains and whose years do not fail. The creation and divine-duration contrast is explicit in both.

relationship: A thousand years and a day in the Lord's reckoning
rationale: The psalm compares a thousand years in God's eyes to yesterday and a night watch. Second Peter repeats the thousand-years/day comparison in both directions while addressing the apparent delay of the promise. The night-watch image remains distinctive to the psalm.

relationship: Passing human life pictured as grass
rationale: The psalm's morning grass image belongs to its account of passing years. Isaiah explicitly calls all flesh grass and contrasts its withering with God's enduring word. The connection uses the grass image; it does not replace the psalm's unusual opening clause with another edition's flood language.

relationship: Blossoming and vanishing life as grass
rationale: Psalm 89 pictures morning blossoming followed by evening drying. Psalm 102 likens human days to grass and a field flower, followed by a passing wind and disappearance. Both develop the short course of flourishing vegetation as an image of mortality, with different descriptions of its passing.

relationship: Wrongdoing exposed before God's sight
rationale: The psalm says God set the community's lawless deeds before Him. Jeremiah says their wrongdoings were not hidden before His eyes. This concerns the visibility of wrongdoing to God; the psalm's separate clause about our age in the light of His face is preserved as supplied.

relationship: Eighty years and diminished human capacities
rationale: The psalm names seventy years, or eighty with strength, amid toil and pain. Barzillai asks how many years remain and describes declining taste and hearing at eighty. His individual account provides a concrete comparison of advanced age, without turning the psalm into a universal lifespan rule.

relationship: Questions concerning the force of divine anger
rationale: The psalm asks who knows the might of God's anger. Nahum asks who can stand before or resist that anger and depicts its destructive force. The rhetorical questions concern human limits before divine wrath, while knowing its might and withstanding it remain different questions.

relationship: Mosaic intercession for relief from divine anger
rationale: The Moses-attributed psalm asks the Lord to return and be moved concerning His servants after its description of wrath. Exodus narrates Moses asking God to cease fierce anger and show mercy concerning His people. The prayers share the intercessory movement without establishing one historical occasion.

relationship: Morning mercy accompanied by exultation
rationale: Psalm 89 reports being filled with God's mercy in the morning and rejoicing. Psalm 58 resolves to exult in His mercy in the morning. The distinctive morning-mercy-and-joy combination corresponds, while the reported past and prospective resolve remain different.

relationship: Same-chapter reversal of afflicted days and years
rationale: The report of gladness in return for days of humiliation and years of evils answers the earlier anger, failed days and painful years. Repeated days-and-years language organizes this internal reversal within the prayer; its supplied past formulations are retained.

relationship: Dwelling within God's protective shelter
rationale: Psalm 90 joins dwelling in the Most High's help with lodging in divine shelter. Psalm 26 describes being hidden and sheltered in God's tent during trouble. Both portray divine protection through a sheltered dwelling, without identifying the psalm's lodging with a particular physical tent.

relationship: God as helper, refuge and object of hope
rationale: The confession in Psalm 90 combines my Helper, my refuge, my God and hope in Him. Psalm 17 combines refuge, rescuer, my God, helper and hope in Him in its longer list of protective titles. The cluster of titles and hope formula supplies the correspondence.

relationship: Rescue from the hunters' trap
rationale: Psalm 90 promises rescue from the hunters' trap. Psalm 123 pictures the rescued community's soul as a bird escaping a shattered hunters' trap. The trap and rescue correspond; the bird and broken-trap details belong to the target.

relationship: Protection pictured beneath God's wings
rationale: Psalm 90 promises overshadowing and hope beneath divine wings. Psalm 16 asks to be guarded and says God will shelter the speaker in the shelter of His wings. Both use the wing-shelter image, while the request and assurances retain their distinct forms.

relationship: Fearless rest and approaching threats
rationale: Psalm 90 speaks of freedom from night terror and the day's missile. Proverbs promises pleasant sleep and freedom from approaching fright or ungodly assault under the Lord's support. The comparison joins protected rest with threatened attack; the target does not supply the missile image.

relationship: Seeing the outcome of sinners' wrongdoing
rationale: Psalm 90 says the protected person will observe sinners' repayment with his eyes. Psalm 36 says the one waiting for the Lord will see when sinners are destroyed. Both expressly describe witnessing judgment; the target additionally speaks of inheriting the land.

relationship: Same-chapter return to refuge and hope
rationale: After the descriptions of danger, verse 9 returns to the opening Most High, refuge and hope vocabulary. This repeated confession links the opening shelter statement to the ensuing protection promises. The verse's changes of address are preserved without assigning every pronoun an inferred speaker.

relationship: A protected dwelling spared the destructive blow
rationale: The psalm promises that a scourge will not approach the dwelling. Exodus describes the Lord preventing the destroyer from entering the blood-marked houses to strike. This is a concrete comparison of protected dwellings, without identifying the psalm's promise with that Passover occasion.

relationship: The angel-command promise quoted in the temptation
rationale: The tempter cites the psalm's command concerning angels when urging Jesus to throw Himself down. Matthew's citation omits the source's all-your-ways clause. Jesus' following refusal to test God governs this narrative use; the quotation is not an endorsement of the tempter's proposed action.

relationship: The lifted hands and stone promise quoted
rationale: Luke's tempter quotes being lifted on angels' hands lest the foot strike a stone. The wording closely corresponds to this psalm unit. The complete temptation context includes Jesus' rejection of putting God to the test, rather than making deliberate danger the promise's application.

relationship: Treading dangerous serpents
rationale: The psalm describes stepping on an asp and basilisk and trampling a lion and dragon. Jesus gives the disciples authority to tread snakes and scorpions. The serpent-treading image corresponds, while the creature lists and the disciples' narrative setting remain distinct.

relationship: Knowing God's name and hoping in Him
rationale: Psalm 90 joins the protected person's hope with knowing God's name. Psalm 9 calls those who know His name to hope in Him and says He has not abandoned His seekers. The shared knowing-name and hope combination is more specific than a general rescue theme.

relationship: Calling in affliction and receiving rescue
rationale: Both join calling upon God in affliction with His rescue. Their final glorifying clauses differ: Psalm 90 has God glorify the rescued person, while Psalm 49 has the rescued person glorify God. The correspondence preserves that reversal of agency.

relationship: Length of days granted by God
rationale: Psalm 90 promises to fill the protected person with length of days. Psalm 20 reports the king asking God for life and receiving length of days. Both explicitly present prolonged life as divinely given, with different beneficiaries and forms of speech.

relationship: Thanksgiving and music to the name of the Most High
rationale: Psalm 91 joins thanks to the Lord with music to the name of the Most High. Psalm 7 likewise joins thanks to the Lord with singing praise to the name of the Lord Most High. The combined acts and divine title form a close verbal parallel.

relationship: Morning mercy in declaration and experience
rationale: Psalm 91 makes declaring divine mercy in the morning part of its thanksgiving. Psalm 89 reports being filled with that mercy in the morning and rejoicing. The morning-mercy wording corresponds, while Psalm 91 adds its distinct declaration of truth by night.

relationship: The ten-stringed psaltery and lyre
rationale: Both specify a ten-stringed psaltery together with a lyre in music offered to God. This is a correspondence of the named instrument combination, without identifying a particular performance or equating every additional musical expression.

relationship: Rejoicing in God's works with different celebrants
rationale: Psalm 91 says God's making gladdened the speaker, who will exult at His handiwork. Psalm 103 says the Lord will rejoice in His works. The shared joy-in-divine-works pattern preserves the difference between the human celebrant and God Himself.

relationship: The depth of divine thought and wisdom
rationale: The psalm calls God's reasonings very deep. Romans praises the depth of His wisdom and knowledge and asks who knew His mind. Both portray divine understanding through depth; Romans adds explicit questions about the limits of human understanding.

relationship: Lawless flourishing pictured as short-lived grass
rationale: Psalm 91 pictures sinners springing up like grass before destruction. Psalm 36 warns against envying evildoers because they will dry up like grass and fall like green plants. The same vegetation image interprets the apparent flourishing of the lawless.

relationship: The scattering of God's opponents
rationale: Psalm 91 predicts the perishing of God's enemies and the scattering of workers of lawlessness. Psalm 67 asks that God arise and His enemies be scattered. The dispersal language corresponds while each verse's subjects and prediction or petition remain intact.

relationship: The raised horn as a personal image of strength
rationale: Psalm 91 says the speaker's horn will be raised like a one-horned creature's. Hannah's song says her horn is exalted in her God. The personal horn-exaltation metaphor corresponds; the psalm's animal comparison and old-age-in-oil clause are not supplied to Hannah's words.

relationship: The righteous person as a flourishing tree
rationale: Psalm 91 compares the righteous to a blossoming palm and a multiplying cedar of Lebanon. Psalm 1 depicts the person who delights in the law as a planted, fruitful tree. Both portray righteous life through sustained tree growth, with distinct species and settings.

relationship: A fruitful tree within God's house
rationale: Psalm 91 places the flourishing trees in the Lord's house and courts. Psalm 51 compares the speaker to a fruitful olive tree in God's house. The shared divine-house and fruitful-tree combination is explicit, while the olive remains distinct from the preceding palm and cedar.

relationship: A favorable old age associated with righteousness
rationale: Within its portrait of the righteous, Psalm 91 describes multiplying and flourishing in a rich old age. Proverbs calls old age a crown of boasting found in ways of righteousness. Both give a positive image of age in relation to righteous living, without equating their tree and crown metaphors.

relationship: God's righteousness excludes injustice
rationale: Psalm 91 declares the Lord upright with no injustice in Him. Deuteronomy calls Him faithful, without unrighteousness, righteous and holy. The explicit denial of injustice alongside divine righteousness forms the comparison.

relationship: Divine kingship and the unshaken world
rationale: Both announce the Lord's reign and connect it with His establishing the inhabited world so that it will not be shaken. Psalm 92 adds clothing and girding with power; Psalm 95 adds the announcement among nations and upright judgment.

relationship: The enduring divine throne
rationale: Psalm 92 joins the throne's readiness from then with God's existence from the age. Lamentations confesses that the Lord will dwell for ever and His throne endures through generations. Both affirm divine rule's duration amid otherwise different poetic settings.

relationship: Rivers personified with voices and hands
rationale: Psalm 92 pictures rivers lifting their voices. Psalm 97 pictures rivers clapping their hands as mountains exult. Both give rivers human expressive action in proclamations of the Lord's rule, one vocal and the other applause; the source's emotion is not otherwise specified.

relationship: Many waters in a portrayal of divine majesty
rationale: Psalm 92 speaks of the voices of many waters, wondrous sea surges and the Lord wondrous on high. Psalm 28 describes the Lord's voice over waters and the Lord over many waters. The combination of many waters, voice language and divine majesty corresponds, with the waters' voices distinct from God's voice.

relationship: Holiness belonging to God's dwelling
rationale: The psalm says sanctity befits the Lord's house. Paul says God's temple is holy and addresses the community as that temple in which His Spirit dwells. The shared holiness of divine dwelling remains distinct from Paul's application of the temple image to people.

relationship: Vengeance belongs to the Lord
rationale: Psalm 93 calls the Lord the God of vengeance. Romans forbids private vengeance and cites the Lord's claim that vengeance and repayment are His. The divine ownership of vengeance connects the texts; Paul's corresponding instruction to believers is stated in its own context.

relationship: Appeal to the Judge of all the earth
rationale: Psalm 93 invokes the Judge of the earth to repay the arrogant. Abraham appeals to the One judging all the earth to do justice in distinguishing righteous and ungodly. Both appeal to God's universal judicial authority, while requesting different judicial outcomes.

relationship: Questioning the boasting of wrongdoers
rationale: Psalm 93 asks how long sinners will boast. Psalm 51 asks why the mighty one boasts in wickedness and lawlessness. Both make wrongful boasting the object of a direct rhetorical challenge, without identifying the psalm's sinners with the person addressed in Psalm 51.

relationship: Oppression of God's people and inheritance
rationale: Psalm 93 says opponents humbled God's people and mistreated His inheritance. Isaiah addresses the daughter of the Chaldeans for defiling His inheritance and showing His people no mercy. The paired people-and-inheritance description and oppressive treatment correspond without identifying the unnamed opponents.

relationship: Violence against the stranger, widow and orphan
rationale: The psalm charges opponents with killing widows, newcomers and orphans. Exodus forbids afflicting the resident foreigner, widow and orphan, and announces divine wrath against violators. The complete vulnerable-group combination and threatened accountability make the legal relation particular.

relationship: Wrongdoers claim the Lord does not see
rationale: Psalm 93 reports the claim that the Lord will not see or understand. Ezekiel reports elders acting secretly and saying the Lord does not see and has abandoned the land. The explicit denial of divine sight corresponds, without equating the two groups or their acts.

relationship: The Creator of hearing and sight
rationale: The psalm asks whether the One who planted the ear and formed the eye can fail to hear or perceive. Proverbs says an ear hears and an eye sees and calls both works of the Lord. The paired organs and divine creation support the psalm's rhetorical argument.

relationship: Human reasonings quoted as the thoughts of the wise
rationale: Paul explicitly cites the Lord's knowledge that thoughts are futile. The psalm says human reasonings; Paul's quoted form says the thoughts of the wise. The quotation is retained with that wording difference and its argument against boasting in human wisdom.

relationship: A beatitude for the person God disciplines
rationale: The psalm calls happy the person the Lord disciplines and teaches. Eliphaz likewise calls happy the person the Lord reproved. This is a comparison of their beatitude wording, not an endorsement of Eliphaz's application to Job; the friends' speech is qualified by the reproof in Job 42:7-8.

relationship: The Lord will not reject His people
rationale: The psalm's assurance that the Lord will not reject His people closely matches Samuel's assurance to Israel. Samuel grounds it in the Lord's great name and gracious choice. The shared refusal-to-reject formula is explicit in both.

relationship: The refusal to reject God's people reaffirmed
rationale: Paul asks whether God rejected His people and answers that He did not reject those He foreknew. This closely corresponds to the psalm's assurance that the Lord will not reject His people. Paul's discussion of Israel and the remnant supplies the target's particular application.

relationship: Divine rescue and the soul's relation to Hades
rationale: Psalm 93 says that without the Lord's help the speaker's soul would almost have sojourned in Hades. Psalm 29 thanks the Lord for bringing his soul up from Hades. Both use the soul-and-Hades image for mortal danger and divine rescue, in counterfactual and retrospective forms.

relationship: Personal images of a shaken foot
rationale: Psalm 93 presents the shaken-foot statement conditionally and follows it with the Lord's helping mercy. Psalm 72 confesses that the feet were almost shaken while envying sinners' peace. The personal foot-instability image corresponds, with the target supplying its own occasion of envy.

relationship: Command or writing used for injustice
rationale: The psalm questions whether a throne of lawlessness shaping toil by command can join God. Isaiah condemns writers of wickedness who turn aside the poor's judgment and exploit widows and orphans. The comparison concerns command or writing associated with injustice, without supplying a particular written ordinance to Isaiah.

relationship: Collective plotting against righteous life
rationale: Psalm 93 describes hunting a righteous person's soul and condemning innocent blood. Proverbs exposes a group's invitation to bloodshed and to hiding a righteous man unjustly in the earth. The shared targeting of righteous life is retained, with judicial condemnation and the criminal invitation distinguished.

relationship: The refuge, helper and hope confession repeated
rationale: Psalm 93 joins the Lord as refuge with God as helper of the speaker's hope. Psalm 90 combines my Helper, my refuge, my God and hope in Him. The repeated cluster of protective titles supplies the correspondence while preserving the different construction of hope.

relationship: Repayment measured by wrongdoing
rationale: Psalm 93 predicts repayment of lawlessness according to wickedness. Psalm 27 petitions for repayment according to opponents' works and the wickedness of their practices. The parallel joins repayment, wrongdoing and the according-to formulation, while prediction and request remain distinct.

relationship: Paired calls to exult and raise a shout
rationale: Psalm 94 calls the community to exult in the Lord and shout to God its Savior. Psalm 80 pairs exultation in God its helper with a shout to the God of Jacob. The paired acclamations correspond without equating their distinct headings or festival contexts.

relationship: Approaching God with thanksgiving and psalms
rationale: Psalm 94 calls for coming before God's face with thanksgiving and psalms. Psalm 99 calls for entering His gates with thanksgiving and courts with hymns. The shared approach-plus-thanksgiving-and-music pattern is explicit, with different descriptions of the place of approach.

relationship: Divine greatness above all gods
rationale: Psalm 94 calls the Lord a great God and great King above all gods. Psalm 95 likewise declares the Lord great and fearsome above all gods. The closely repeated greatness-and-above-all-gods formula receives a royal designation in Psalm 94 and a fearsome designation in Psalm 95.

relationship: The earth and mountains in God's hand
rationale: The psalm places earth's ends in God's hand and assigns Him the mountain heights. Isaiah asks who measured earth with a handful and weighed the mountains. The earth-and-mountain pairing with divine handling corresponds; possession in the psalm differs from Isaiah's measurement imagery.

relationship: The maker of sea and dry land
rationale: The psalm says God made the sea and formed dry land. Jonah identifies the God he worships as the One who made sea and dry land. The paired creation confession is nearly the same, spoken in praise in the psalm and during Jonah's sea voyage in the narrative.

relationship: God's people described as His flock
rationale: The psalm joins He is our God with the people of His pasture and sheep of His hand. Ezekiel identifies Israel as His people, His sheep and flock, and names Himself their God. The people-flock-God combination corresponds while the hand and pasture wording remains the psalm's own.

relationship: The Today appeal quoted by Hebrews
rationale: Hebrews introduces the Holy Spirit's speech with the psalm's closing appeal to hear His voice today. This citation takes up the final clause of the source unit; the preceding people-and-sheep confession remains the psalm's immediate context.

relationship: The wilderness hardening warning quoted
rationale: Hebrews quotes the command not to harden hearts as in the provocation and wilderness testing. The close wording links its exhortation against unbelief to this psalm warning, while the larger Hebrews argument supplies the new audience and application.

relationship: The ancestors' testing and sight of God's works quoted
rationale: Hebrews repeats the ancestors testing God and seeing His works. Its first-person Me makes the divine object of the testing explicit. This is part of its sustained quotation of the psalm rather than an independently identified new wilderness incident.

relationship: Forty years and the wandering generation in the quotation
rationale: Hebrews retains forty years, divine indignation, wandering hearts and ignorance of God's ways. In its sequence forty years completes the preceding saw-My-works clause before Therefore I was indignant; the psalm directly places the forty years with God's vexation. The shared citation preserves that difference.

relationship: Forty years of wilderness judgment
rationale: The psalm remembers forty years of divine vexation with the generation that strays in heart. Numbers announces forty years in the wilderness bearing sins and knowing God's anger. The stated duration, wilderness generation and divine anger provide the narrative correspondence without making every clause an exact quotation.

relationship: The oath excluding entry into God's rest quoted
rationale: Hebrews repeats the sworn declaration that the rebellious will not enter God's rest. It subsequently discusses those whose bodies fell in the wilderness and their unbelief. The target explicitly receives the psalm's oath into that argument.

relationship: The rest oath reused alongside creation's Sabbath
rationale: Hebrews repeats the psalm's exclusion oath while discussing believers entering rest and God's seventh-day rest. The connection is this explicit reuse and interpretation; it does not reduce all of Hebrews' rest language to a single geographical destination.

relationship: The all-earth singing summons in the Chronicles song
rationale: The psalm's call for all the earth to sing to the Lord corresponds to the same summons in David's appointed praise before the ark. The psalm adds a new song and a post-captivity house-building heading; those different settings are preserved rather than identified.

relationship: House-building after captivity accompanied by praise
rationale: The heading places the song when the house was being built after captivity. Ezra narrates returned captives beginning work on God's house and communal praise when the foundation was laid. The building, return and praise setting corresponds, without proving this exact ceremony is the heading's occasion.

relationship: Salvation proclaimed from day to day
rationale: The psalm calls for announcing the good news of God's salvation day after day. Chronicles' song likewise calls for proclaiming His salvation from day to day. The distinctive salvation-and-daily-proclamation phrase forms the comparison.

relationship: Wonders recounted among all peoples
rationale: The psalm calls for God's glory to be announced among nations and His wonders among all peoples. Chronicles calls for His works to be known among peoples and His wonders recounted to everyone. These are parallel universal proclamation directives; glory and works remain distinct words.

relationship: The great and fearsome Lord in the parallel song
rationale: Both declare the Lord great, greatly to be praised and fearsome above all gods. The close multi-clause wording belongs to the extended correspondence between this psalm and Chronicles' song, without identifying their stated occasions.

relationship: The nations' gods contrasted with the heavenly Creator
rationale: Both contrast the gods of the nations with the God who made heaven. The psalm calls those gods demons; Chronicles calls them idols. The creator contrast is retained with the different descriptions of the nations' gods made explicit.

relationship: Qualities before God and in His place
rationale: Both arrange qualities before God and qualities in His place. The psalm gives thanksgiving and beauty, then holiness and magnificence in His sanctuary; Chronicles gives glory and praise, then strength and boasting in His place. The parallel structure preserves these lexical differences.

relationship: Families of nations summoned to bring glory
rationale: Both address families of nations and repeat the summons to bring or give to the Lord. The psalm pairs glory with honor; Chronicles pairs glory with strength. The shared address and repeated imperative are retained without substituting one second object for the other.

relationship: Name-glory, offerings and approach to God
rationale: Both join glory for God's name with bringing offerings and approaching Him. The psalm says sacrifices and entry to His courts; Chronicles says gifts brought before Him and then worship in His holy courts. The ordered ritual actions correspond with their supplied differences.

relationship: Worship in holy courts and the earth's response
rationale: The psalm commands bowing in God's holy court and that all earth be shaken. Chronicles likewise places bowing in His holy courts beside a call for all earth to fear before Him. Court worship and worldwide response correspond, while shaking and fear are different formulations.

relationship: The stable world and announcement of divine reign
rationale: The psalm joins announcing the Lord's kingship among nations with the established world that will not be shaken. Chronicles places the earth being set right and unshaken beside saying among nations that the Lord reigns. The matching clauses occur in a different order and mood.

relationship: Heaven, earth and the full sea responding
rationale: Both summon or describe heaven's gladness, earth's exultation and the sea with its fullness. The psalm says the sea should be shaken; Chronicles says it shall resound. The sequence of cosmic participants is shared without making those sea verbs identical.

relationship: Field and forest in the parallel praise sequence
rationale: The psalm moves from rejoicing plains and their contents to exulting woodland trees. Chronicles moves from the tree of the field and everything in it to glad forest trees. Their field-to-forest sequence corresponds while the supplied plains and tree-of-field wording remains distinct.

relationship: The Lord's coming to judge the earth
rationale: Both explain nature's rejoicing by the Lord's coming to judge the earth. The psalm repeats that He is coming and specifies righteousness and truth; Chronicles says He has come and does not include those final qualifications in this unit.

relationship: Islands included in worldwide rejoicing and praise
rationale: Psalm 96 calls the earth and many islands to rejoice at the Lord's kingship. Isaiah's new hymn addresses the earth's extremity and island inhabitants and announces praise in the islands. Both expressly extend the celebration to islands, without assigning the psalm's land-establishment heading a historical event.

relationship: Righteousness and judgment establish the divine throne
rationale: Both place righteousness and judgment in the establishment or preparation of God's throne. Psalm 96 surrounds Him with cloud and gloom; Psalm 88 has mercy and truth go before His face. The shared throne formula is distinguished from their surrounding imagery.

relationship: Fire preceding the divine approach
rationale: Psalm 96 describes fire going before God and burning His enemies. Psalm 49 describes God coming manifestly with fire burning before Him and a surrounding tempest. Both place fire before the approaching God, with different descriptions of its surroundings and effects.

relationship: World-illuminating lightning and the shaken earth
rationale: Both say divine lightning shone upon the inhabited world and that the earth shook. Psalm 76 additionally describes the voice of thunder in the wheel. The lightning-and-earth response is a close verbal parallel, with that additional image left in the target.

relationship: Wax-melting imagery at the Lord's advent
rationale: The psalm has mountains melt like wax before the Lord. Micah describes the Lord descending, mountains shaken beneath Him and valleys melting like wax before fire. The wax-melting image accompanies divine approach in both; mountains and valleys are not conflated.

relationship: The heavens announce God's righteousness
rationale: Both expressly give the heavens the action of announcing God's righteousness. Psalm 49 connects this with God as judge; Psalm 96 joins it to all peoples seeing His glory. The shared announcement clause retains its different neighboring explanations.

relationship: The command for angelic worship echoed in Hebrews
rationale: The psalm commands all His angels to bow down. Hebrews commands all God's angels to worship when the firstborn is brought into the inhabited world. The angelic worship summons closely corresponds; this does not claim it is the only related scriptural formulation.

relationship: Zion and Judea's daughters rejoice at God's judgments
rationale: Both join Zion's rejoicing with the exultation of Judea's daughters because of the Lord's judgments. Psalm 96 reports that Zion heard and rejoiced; Psalm 47 frames the shared response as a summons. The location, participants and reason all correspond.

relationship: The Most High over all the earth
rationale: Both identify the Lord as Most High over all the earth. Psalm 96 adds His exaltation above all gods, while Psalm 82 asks opponents to recognize His name and unique height. The shared worldwide Most High formula is explicit.

relationship: Love and hatred in moral allegiance
rationale: The psalm commands those loving the Lord to hate evil. Amos quotes We have hated evil things and loved good things while urging restoration of judgment. Both pair love and hatred with moral allegiance; Amos's reported words are not converted into the psalm's imperative, and the objects of love differ.

relationship: Light associated with righteous life
rationale: Psalm 96 says light has dawned for the righteous. Proverbs describes righteous ways shining like light and advancing toward the day. Both portray righteous life through illumination, with a light dawning for people distinguished from their ways themselves shining.

relationship: Thanksgiving at the remembrance of holiness
rationale: Both call for thanks at the remembrance of God's holiness, addressed to righteous or holy people in a context of praise. The distinctive remembrance-of-holiness thanksgiving formula is repeated, with differing surrounding commands.

relationship: The holy arm and divine salvation
rationale: Psalm 97 says God's right hand and holy arm won salvation for Him. Isaiah says the Lord will uncover His holy arm before nations and the earth's ends will see salvation from God. The holy-arm and salvation combination is explicit, with achieved salvation and future manifestation distinguished.

relationship: Salvation made visible before the nations
rationale: Psalm 97 reports salvation made known and righteousness revealed before the nations. Isaiah promises the unveiling of God's holy arm before all nations and salvation seen at earth's ends. Both present divine rescue publicly to nations; righteousness and the holy arm remain their distinct revealed objects.

relationship: Earth's ends seeing God's salvation
rationale: The psalm reports all earth's ends seeing the salvation of our God. Isaiah predicts all earth's ends seeing salvation from God. The close concluding formula corresponds, while the psalm additionally names remembered mercy to Jacob and truth to Israel.

relationship: All the earth summoned to shout and make music
rationale: Both address all the earth with a shout to God and an accompanying call to music. Psalm 97 adds singing and exultation; Psalm 65 specifies music to His name and glory to His praise. The repeated worldwide acclamation-and-music pattern supplies the link.

relationship: Music to God with a lyre
rationale: Psalm 97 repeats the lyre in its command to make music to the Lord. Psalm 146 likewise commands music to God with a lyre after beginning with thanksgiving. The particular instrument and God-directed musical command correspond without identifying a single performance.

relationship: Trumpets made of hammered work
rationale: The psalm names hammered trumpets in its acclamation before the Lord as King. Numbers orders two silver trumpets made of hammered work, within instructions that include their use at feasts and offerings. The manufacture and instrument type correspond; the psalm's horn trumpet is a separate named instrument.

relationship: The sea and its fullness in the creation summons
rationale: Both call for the sea and all that fills it to be shaken. Psalm 97 adds the inhabited world and its dwellers, whereas Psalm 95 first calls heaven and earth to rejoice. The closely repeated sea clause links the two creation-wide summonses.

relationship: Clapping nature and rejoicing mountains
rationale: Psalm 97 has rivers clap their hands and mountains exult. Isaiah has mountains and hills leap in joy and field trees clap their branches. Both combine joyful mountains with clapping nonhuman creation, preserving rivers versus trees and hands versus branches.

relationship: The repeated closing announcement of world judgment
rationale: Both close their creation rejoicing with the Lord's coming to judge the earth and world in righteousness. Psalm 97 says He has come and peoples will be judged with uprightness; Psalm 95 says He is coming and gives His truth. The parallel ending preserves tense and final-attribute differences.

relationship: The Lord seated upon the cherubim
rationale: Psalm 98 describes the reigning Lord seated upon the cherubim. The account in 1 Samuel uses the same throne description when the Lord's ark is carried from Shiloh. The shared divine title does not identify the psalm with that battle or endorse the Israelites' expectation that bringing the ark guarantees victory.

relationship: The divine name as holy and fearsome
rationale: Psalm 98 calls for thanks to the great name because it is fearsome and holy. Psalm 110 concludes its redemption-and-covenant statement by calling His name holy and fearsome. The paired attributes explicitly qualify the divine name in both.

relationship: Kingship, righteousness and preparation
rationale: Psalm 98 says the King's honor loves judgment and that God prepared uprightness. Proverbs says a ruling throne is prepared with righteousness and evil is abhorrent to a king. Both connect kingship, preparation and righteous order: uprightness is prepared in the psalm, while a throne is prepared with righteousness in the proverb.

relationship: Bowing toward the place of God's feet
rationale: Psalm 98 commands bowing at God's footstool. Psalm 131 resolves to enter His dwellings and bow toward the place where His feet stood. The location associated with divine feet and the act of bowing correspond; no independent object identity is asserted for the footstool.

relationship: Samuel calls upon the Lord and is heard
rationale: The psalm names Samuel among those who called on God and were heard. The narrative reports Israel requesting his intercession, his cry for Israel and the Lord hearing him. The named person and call-and-hearing action provide the concrete narrative link; the psalm also names Moses and Aaron.

relationship: Divine speech in the pillar of cloud
rationale: The psalm describes speech to them in a pillar of cloud. Exodus describes the pillar descending at the tent while God speaks with Moses. The cloud-pillar and speech correspond; Moses is the target's named recipient, and Samuel is not inserted into that scene through the psalm's collective pronoun.

relationship: Graciousness together with judgment
rationale: The psalm joins God's graciousness with vengeance for practices. Numbers places God's gracious answer to Moses beside exclusion from the land for those who repeatedly tested Him. Both hold graciousness and consequences together, without equating all referents of the psalm's pronouns with that congregation.

relationship: Same-chapter framing by exaltation and bowing
rationale: Verses 5 and 9 repeat Exalt the Lord our God, the call to bow, and the reason of holiness. Footstool and holy mountain give the two locations. The refrain frames the intervening account of mediators calling upon God and His answer and judgment.

relationship: The all-earth acclamation repeated
rationale: Psalm 99 opens its thanksgiving with the command that all the earth shout to the Lord. Psalm 97 uses the same all-earth shout to God before further musical commands. The concise worldwide acclamation formula links these neighboring praise psalms.

relationship: Serving the Lord with gladness
rationale: Psalm 99 commands service to the Lord with gladness. Deuteronomy identifies failure to serve Him with gladness and a good heart as grounds for the ensuing judgment. The same service-and-gladness combination appears as positive summons and reproach for its absence.

relationship: The Creator's people and the sheep of His pasture
rationale: Psalm 99 joins God's making us with His people and the sheep of His pasture. Psalm 94 likewise joins the Lord who made us with our God, the people of His pasture and sheep of His hand. The combined creation-and-flock confession corresponds, including the differing hand clause.

relationship: Entering the Lord's gates with thanksgiving
rationale: Psalm 99 commands entry through God's gates with thanksgiving. Psalm 117 requests the opening of righteousness's gates and says the entrant will thank the Lord, then names the Lord's gate. The gate, entry and thanksgiving sequence is explicit in both.

relationship: Enduring mercy and truth in praise
rationale: Psalm 99 joins everlasting mercy with truth through generations. Psalm 116 joins mercy grown strong over the people with the Lord's truth remaining for ever. Both pair mercy and truth in praise; the duration clauses are retained with the attributes to which each text attaches them.

relationship: Mercy and judgment paired
rationale: The speaker will sing mercy and judgment to the Lord. Psalm 32 explicitly says God loves mercy and judgment. The same ethical pair is the song's subject in one passage and the object of divine love in the other.

relationship: Davidic walking with an upright heart
rationale: The Davidic psalm reports walking in innocence of heart within the house. God tells Solomon to walk as David walked, with holiness of heart and uprightness. The named Davidic frame and walking-heart combination correspond, without making the household setting the same as Solomon's temple scene.

relationship: Personal refusal of wrongdoing and hatred of evildoers
rationale: Psalm 100 says the speaker did not set a lawless matter before his eyes and hated transgressors. Psalm 25 says he did not sit with emptiness and hated an assembly of evildoers. The paired avowal of refusal and hatred corresponds while their specified acts remain different.

relationship: Speech against the neighbor excluded
rationale: Psalm 100 reports driving away one speaking secretly against his neighbor. Psalm 14's qualified dweller does not act deceitfully with his tongue or take up reproach against those nearest him. Both exclude damaging neighbor-directed speech from accepted conduct, with their different actions and agents preserved.

relationship: Blameless walking as a qualification for dwelling and service
rationale: Psalm 100 chooses faithful people to sit with the speaker and the blameless walker to minister to him. Psalm 14 asks who may dwell with the Lord and answers with one walking blamelessly. The shared admission criterion is explicit; the speaker's attendants and God's dwelling guests are distinct roles.

relationship: Wrongdoers excluded from dwelling and presence
rationale: Psalm 100 says a practitioner of arrogance did not dwell in the speaker's house and a speaker of unjust things did not prosper before his eyes. Psalm 5 says an evildoer will not sojourn with God and the lawless will not remain before His eyes. The dwelling-and-before-the-eyes pattern is shared, with human household and divine presence distinguished.

relationship: Morning administration in Davidic settings
rationale: The Davidic psalm reports morning killing of sinners to remove lawlessness from the Lord's city. Jeremiah commands the house of David to judge in the morning and rescue the plundered. The morning and Davidic public-justice setting corresponds; reported killing and commanded rescue are not equated.

relationship: Pouring out a plea in despondency
rationale: The heading describes a poor person becoming despondent and pouring out a petition before the Lord. Psalm 141 resolves to pour out a plea before Him and recalls the spirit failing within. The pouring-prayer and inward-collapse combination corresponds without identifying the anonymous sufferer with David's cave setting.

relationship: The face, affliction and swift-hearing plea
rationale: Both ask God not to turn His face away and join affliction with a plea to hear quickly. Psalm 101 additionally specifies the ear inclined in affliction and quick hearing when called. The shared face-affliction-hearing sequence makes the parallel particular.

relationship: Bones scorched by heat in a lament
rationale: The psalm describes bones scorched like kindling. Job says his bones are scorched from heat within his own lament. The particular heated-bones image corresponds, while the kindling comparison and vanished days like smoke remain the psalm's distinct images.

relationship: Same-chapter recurrence of grass drying up
rationale: The struck and dried heart is likened to grass in verse 5; verse 12 again says the speaker dried up like grass while describing declining days. The repeated drying-grass simile links bodily affliction with the poem's later statement of temporal frailty.

relationship: The wasted body with flesh or skin against bones
rationale: The psalm says the bone clung to the speaker's flesh amid groaning and forgotten food. Lamentations describes skin clinging to bones, drying like wood, in a famine context. Both depict bodily wasting through the bone-covering relationship; flesh and skin and the respective circumstances remain distinct.

relationship: Bird imagery with wilderness or deserted land
rationale: The psalm compares the speaker to a wilderness pelican and a night raven on a house site. Isaiah places birds including ravens in land destined for enduring desolation. The bird imagery and wilderness or deserted settings offer a limited poetic comparison; the source's house site is not declared identical with Isaiah's deserted land. Night raven and raven are not asserted to be identical species, nor is the sufferer's situation identified with that judgment.

relationship: Tears incorporated into food and drink imagery
rationale: Psalm 101 reports ashes eaten like bread and drink mixed with weeping. Psalm 79 asks whether God will feed bread of tears and give tears to drink by measure. Both combine bread, drink and grief, with ashes and the measure kept in their respective texts.

relationship: Being cast down after elevation
rationale: The afflicted speaker says God lifted him and then dashed him down. Psalm 72 describes God casting down deceitful people when they were lifted up. The vertical reversal corresponds; comparison of the image does not assign the target's moral characterization of the wicked to the source's complainant.

relationship: Brief life pictured with vegetation and a shadow
rationale: The psalm joins days bending like a shadow with the speaker drying like grass. Job describes short mortal life as a fallen flower and a fleeing shadow. Both combine vegetation and shadow images for mortality, retaining the different plants and verbs.

relationship: God's memorial through generations
rationale: The psalm confesses the Lord's perpetual endurance and memorial from generation to generation. God's speech to Moses names His everlasting name and memorial from generation to generation. The repeated memorial-and-generations formula supplies the close verbal connection.

relationship: Renewed compassion for Zion and Jerusalem
rationale: Psalm 101 announces that the time for compassion on Zion has come. Zechariah moves from asking how long Jerusalem will lack mercy to God's promise to return in compassion and again have mercy on Zion. The shared focus is compassion for Zion and its announced arrival; Zechariah supplies the explicit preceding complaint and its stated year.

relationship: Concern for the material remains of Jerusalem
rationale: The psalm says God's servants took pleasure in Zion's stones and will have compassion on her dust. Nehemiah grieves over the desolated ancestral city and asks to rebuild it. Their concern for the city's material setting supplies the comparison; stones and dust remain distinct from the narrative's tombs and burned gates.

relationship: All earth's kings respond to the Lord's glory
rationale: Psalm 101 anticipates nations fearing the Lord's name and all earth's kings His glory. Psalm 137 asks all earth's kings to thank Him for heard words and to sing in His ways because His glory is great. The shared worldwide royal response to divine glory takes different forms: fear in the source and song in the target.

relationship: The Lord builds Zion or Jerusalem
rationale: Psalm 101 says the Lord will build Zion; Psalm 146 says the Lord builds Jerusalem and will gather Israel's dispersed. The divine builder and the holy city correspond. The source additionally describes His appearing in glory rather than the target's gathering clause.

relationship: Regard for prayer and hearing of the needy
rationale: Psalm 101 pairs regard for the lowly's prayer with not treating their petition as nothing. Psalm 68 pairs hearing the needy with not despising His bound ones. The paired divine attention and refusal of disregard correspond, with lowly petitioners, needy people and bound ones kept as each passage names them.

relationship: Divine acts transmitted to a future generation
rationale: The psalm commands a written record for another generation and says the people being created will praise. Psalm 77 transmits divine works to sons yet to be born so they may hope in God. Both address a future audience, with writing and repeated telling, and created people and future sons, distinguished.

relationship: Looking from the holy heavenly dwelling
rationale: Psalm 101 says the Lord looked from His holy height and from heaven upon earth. Deuteronomy petitions Him to look from His holy house, from heaven, and bless Israel and the land. The holy heavenly vantage and downward attention correspond, in report and petition respectively.

relationship: Groaning prisoners and the sons of those put to death
rationale: Psalm 101 joins hearing the groaning of those in bonds with releasing sons of those put to death. Psalm 78 asks that the same groaning enter God's presence and that He preserve sons of those put to death. The two-part formulation is close; the sons are not replaced with people merely sentenced to death.

relationship: The Lord's name proclaimed in Zion's praise
rationale: Psalm 101 states the purpose of announcing the Lord's name in Zion and His praise in Jerusalem. Isaiah calls for His name and deeds to be proclaimed and for Zion's inhabitants to rejoice. The name-proclamation and Zion-praise combination corresponds without identifying a single occasion.

relationship: Peoples gathered to seek and serve God in Jerusalem
rationale: The psalm places gathered peoples and kingdoms serving the Lord after the proclamation in Zion and Jerusalem. Zechariah describes many peoples and nations coming to seek His presence in Jerusalem. The multinational gathering and city-directed worship correspond, while serving and seeking remain distinct expressions.

relationship: Asking to know the brief measure of one's days
rationale: The psalm's direct speech asks to be told the fewness of my days. Psalm 38 asks God to make known life's limit and number of days. The requests concerning life's measure correspond; the source's opening he and him are not assigned unexpressed identities.

relationship: The fear of losing the remaining span of life
rationale: Psalm 101 asks not to be taken up at the halfway point of the speaker's days. Hezekiah's prayer speaks of leaving remaining years behind at the height of his days and Hades' gates. The untimely interruption of life corresponds without identifying the psalm's sufferer as Hezekiah.

relationship: The foundation of earth and heavens quoted in Hebrews
rationale: Hebrews quotes the Lord founding earth in the beginning and the heavens as works of His hands. The passage belongs to its scriptural presentation concerning the Son. The source's creation statement and the target's reception of it are both explicit.

relationship: The perishing heavens and garment image quoted
rationale: Hebrews repeats the created things perishing while the Lord remains, their growing old like a garment and their change. The psalm says He will change them like a cloak; Hebrews says He will roll them up like a cloak and they will be changed. Those verbs are preserved.

relationship: Unchanging identity and unfailing years quoted
rationale: Hebrews reproduces the concluding assertion that Thou art the same and Thy years will not fail. It follows the quoted garment imagery in the target and forms part of the contrast between the enduring Son and created things in that chapter.

relationship: Servants' offspring dwelling in restored Zion
rationale: Psalm 101 ends with servants' children dwelling and their offspring established for ever. Psalm 68 joins God's saving Zion and rebuilding Judea's cities with His servants' offspring possessing it and lovers of His name dwelling there. The restoration, servants' offspring and continuing dwelling cluster corresponds.
